etymology: From Latin musica and English music: one who makes or leads song with voice or instrument. Scripture names singers, players, and chief musicians as appointed servants, not as a secular entertainment caste.
biblical_def: A musician in Israel is a man set to sound praise under order. David appointed Levites to be singers with psalteries, harps, and cymbals, lifting the voice with joy (1 Chr 15:16). The procession of God has singers before and players after (Ps 68:25). The office is ministry: skill offered to the LORD, not self-display. Amos rebukes men who invent instruments of music for their own ease while the nation is at ease in Zion (Amos 6:5). Music is not neutral; it either serves the Name or serves the belly.

etymology: From Hebrew Pelishtim, the sea-people settled on the coastal plain of Canaan — Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath. In later English, also a slur for the coarse or uncultured; that later sense is not the biblical one.
biblical_def: The Philistine is Israel’s near enemy on the western plain, a people with iron, champions, and gods. Goliath of Gath came out as their champion (1 Sam 17:4). David met him not as a better technician of war but in the name of the LORD of hosts (1 Sam 17:45). The Philistine is not a metaphor for bad taste. He is a nation that defied Israel’s God and was judged in history.

corruption_summary: Modern English turned Philistine into a class insult for the uncultured, emptying the word of covenant history and leaving only snobbery.
corruption_paragraphs: Critics and campuses use philistine for the man who will not applaud their art. That is a theft. Scripture’s Philistine is a people with cities, iron, and idols who opposed the LORD’s Israel. Aesthetic contempt is not exegesis.
The second inversion is to treat every cultural outsider as Goliath and every insider as David. Recover the text: the issue is defiance of the LORD of hosts, not failure to like the current gallery.

roots_lines: Hebrew Pelishtim — the Philistines of the coastal pentapolis.

usage: A Philistine in Scripture is a coastal enemy of Israel, not a man with bad taste.

Do not use the Bible’s national name as a campus insult.

etymology: From Old English great plus the abstract suffix -ness: the quality of being large, high, or eminent. Scripture uses it first of the LORD, then of His acts, then only secondarily of men.
biblical_def: Greatness belongs first to God. Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; His greatness is unsearchable (Ps 145:3). Praise Him according to His excellent greatness (Ps 150:2). The New Testament names the exceeding greatness of His power toward those who believe (Eph 1:19). Human greatness is derivative and judged: a man is not great because he is famous, funded, or followed.

etymology: Older English for fornication and harlotry, from whore. In the prophets it regularly names covenant infidelity — going after other gods as a wife goes after other men.
biblical_def: Whoredom is sexual unfaithfulness and, in Israel’s prophets, the same pattern aimed at idols. Judah trusted her own beauty and played the harlot (Ezek 16:15). The spirit of whoredoms caused the people to err from under their God (Hos 4:12). Through the lightness of her whoredom she defiled the land and committed adultery with stones and stocks (Jer 3:9). The word is not Victorian shock; it is covenant language for body and altar alike.

The other theft is to keep the sexual sin and deny the idolatry. Stones and stocks were lovers. Recover both: the body and the altar are under the same covenant.

etymology: From Latin persequi — to follow after, to hunt down. In Scripture it is hostile pursuit of the righteous, not mere disagreement.
biblical_def: To persecute is to hunt a man for righteousness’ sake. Christ commands love of enemies and prayer for those who persecute (Matt 5:44). The servant is not greater than his lord: if they persecuted Him, they will persecute His people (John 15:20). All who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2 Tim 3:12). The word is not a trophy for every bruised ego; it is the world’s war on godliness.

etymology: From heaven plus -ly: of or belonging to heaven. In the New Testament it marks the realm, origin, and quality of God’s gifts over against the earthly.
biblical_def: Heavenly names what is from God’s realm, not what feels pretty. The Father has blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ (Eph 1:3). Believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). Christ distinguishes earthly things from heavenly things (John 3:12). The word is not a synonym for nice, aesthetic, or vaguely spiritual.

etymology: Old English wund: a blow’s opening in flesh. Scripture uses it of body, of the Servant, and of a people’s hurt that the LORD binds up.
biblical_def: A wound is real damage, not a metaphor first. The Servant was wounded for our transgressions (Isa 53:5). The LORD heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds (Ps 147:3). He promises to restore health and heal wounds even when Zion is called Outcast (Jer 30:17). The gospel does not deny wounds; it names their cause and their Healer.

etymology: From English beauty: full of that which pleases by fitness, proportion, or glory. Scripture locates beauty first in the LORD and in His timing, not in the mirror as a god.
biblical_def: Beautiful is what God makes fitting in its time (Eccl 3:11). David desired to behold the beauty of the LORD in His temple (Ps 27:4). The Song can say of covenant love, thou art all fair, there is no spot in thee (Song 4:7). Beauty is not banned; it is ordered. Trusting one’s own beauty as capital is the path Ezekiel names as harlotry (see whoredom). The standard is the LORD’s beauty, not the market’s face.
